CHAPTER 2.2 · LEARNING AREA 2

CHAPTER 2.2 · LEARNING AREA 2 · DECEMBER

Cone and sphere

An ice-cream cone, a party hat, a heap of sand on a building site: these are cones. A football, a marble and the Earth are almost exactly spheres. You learn how to roll the curved surface of a cone from a sector of a circle, how to calculate the surface area and the volume of cone and sphere, and how to get the radius of a sphere back from its volume.

12 LESSONS3 UNITS2 LABS
WHAT YOU WILL LEARN IN THIS CHAPTER
  • tell apart the radius, the height and the slant height of a circular cone and calculate them with Pythagoras
  • draw the curved surface as a sector of a circle
  • calculate the surface area and the volume of a cone
  • calculate the surface area and the volume of a sphere
  • find the radius of a sphere from its volume with the cube root

$2 \cdot \pi \cdot 5 \approx 31.42$ cm

A cylinder has $r = 2$ cm and $h = 5$ cm. What is its volume? Round to two decimal places.

$\pi \cdot 4 \cdot 5 = 20\pi \approx 62.83\,\text{cm}^3$

What is $2^3$?

$2 \cdot 2 \cdot 2 = 8$

UNIT 14 LESSONS

1The circular cone

The paper hat is a circular cone: it has a circle as its base and comes together at the top in an apex. Its curved surface used to be a sector of a circle. The radius of the paper circle becomes the slant height of the hat, the arc of the sector becomes the circumference of the base circle.

KEY POINT · THE CIRCULAR CONE

A right circular cone has a circle with the radius $r$ as its base. The apex lies at the height $h$ straight above the centre. Every line from the apex to the base circle is a slant height $s$.

The height, the radius and the slant height form a right triangle: $\;s^2 = r^2 + h^2$.

Unrolled, the curved surface is a sector with the radius $s$. Its arc is as long as the circumference $2\pi r$ of the base circle, its angle at the centre is $\;\varphi = 360^\circ \cdot \dfrac{r}{s}$.

Always: $s$ is the hypotenuse, so it is longer than $r$ and longer than $h$.

Half a circle: if $s = 2r$, then $\varphi = 180^\circ$: the curved surface is a semicircle.

INTERACTIVE · THE TRIANGLE IN THE CONE

Change the radius and the height. The height, the radius and the slant height always form a right triangle.

EXAMPLE 1 · THE ICE-CREAM CONE

An ice-cream cone has a radius of 3 cm at the top and is 10 cm high. How long is its slant height?

$s = \sqrt{3^2 + 10^2} = \sqrt{109}$

$s \approx 10.44$ cm

EXAMPLE 2 · THE NET OF A CONE

Draw the net of a cone with $r = 3$ cm and $s = 5$ cm. What is the angle at the centre of the curved surface? How high is the cone?

$\varphi = 360^\circ \cdot \tfrac{3}{5} = 216^\circ$. Draw a sector with the radius 5 cm and $216^\circ$, and next to it a circle with a radius of 3 cm.

$h = \sqrt{25 - 9} = 4$ cm

EXERCISES

Calculate the missing measurement of a cone: a) $r = 5$ cm, $h = 12$ cm, $s = \;?$   b) $s = 10$ cm, $r = 6$ cm, $h = \;?$

a) $s = \sqrt{25 + 144} = 13$ cm   b) $h = \sqrt{100 - 36} = 8$ cm

Calculate the angle at the centre of the curved surface: a) $r = 4$ cm, $s = 8$ cm   b) $r = 2$ cm, $s = 6$ cm

a) $180^\circ$ (a semicircle)   b) $120^\circ$

At what angle does the slant height of the ice-cream cone from example 1 ($r = 3$ cm, $h = 10$ cm) slope against the base?

$\tan \alpha = \tfrac{10}{3}$, $\alpha \approx 73.3^\circ$

Draw the net of a cone with $r = 2$ cm and $h = 4.5$ cm. First calculate $s$ and $\varphi$.

$s = \sqrt{4 + 20.25} \approx 4.92$ cm, $\varphi = 360^\circ \cdot \tfrac{2}{4.92} \approx 146^\circ$.

The curved surface of a cone is rolled from a semicircle with a radius of 12 cm. What are the radius and the height of the cone?

$s = 12$ cm. The arc $\pi \cdot 12$ becomes the circumference $2\pi r$, so $r = 6$ cm. $h = \sqrt{144 - 36} = \sqrt{108} \approx 10.39$ cm.

TEST YOURSELF!

$r = 6$ cm, $h = 8$ cm. How long is $s$?

$\sqrt{36 + 64} = 10$ cm

$r = 3$ cm, $s = 5$ cm. What is the angle at the centre of the curved surface?

$360^\circ \cdot \tfrac35 = 216^\circ$

$s = 13$ cm, $r = 5$ cm. How high is the cone?

$\sqrt{169 - 25} = 12$ cm

UNIT 24 LESSONS

2Surface area and volume of the cone

The content of the cone fits exactly three times into the cylinder with the same radius and the same height, just as with pyramid and prism. The cone is something like a pyramid with a great many lateral faces.

KEY POINT · SURFACE AREA AND VOLUME OF THE CONE

Curved surface: $\;M = \pi \cdot r \cdot s$   ·   Surface area: $\;O = \pi r^2 + \pi r s = \pi r \cdot (r + s)$

Volume: $\;V = \tfrac13 \cdot \pi r^2 \cdot h$, one third of the cylinder with the same radius and the same height.

Mass: $\;m = \varrho \cdot V$

Why $\pi r s$? The curved surface is a sector of the circle with the radius $s$. Its share of the whole circle is $\tfrac{r}{s}$: $\;\pi s^2 \cdot \tfrac{r}{s} = \pi r s$.

Two lengths: for the volume you need $h$, for the curved surface $s$.

INTERACTIVE · CALCULATING THE CONE

Change the radius and the height. Slant height, surface area and volume are calculated along.

EXAMPLE 3 · SURFACE AREA AND VOLUME

A cone has $r = 3$ cm and $h = 4$ cm. Calculate $s$, $O$ and $V$.

$s = 5$ cm. $\;M = \pi \cdot 3 \cdot 5 \approx 47.12\,\text{cm}^2$, $\;O = \pi \cdot 9 + 47.12 \approx 75.40\,\text{cm}^2$.

$V = \tfrac13 \cdot \pi \cdot 9 \cdot 4 = 12\pi \approx 37.70\,\text{cm}^3$

EXAMPLE 4 · THE HEAP OF SAND

A heap of sand is a cone with a diameter of 6 m and a height of 1.80 m. How much sand is it? How heavy is it ($\varrho = 1.5\,\tfrac{\text{t}}{\text{m}^3}$)?

$V = \tfrac13 \cdot \pi \cdot 3^2 \cdot 1.8 \approx 16.96\,\text{m}^3$. $\;m = 1.5 \cdot 16.96 \approx 25.4$ t.

About 17 m³ of sand with a mass of roughly 25 t.

EXERCISES

A cone has $r = 5$ cm and $h = 12$ cm. Calculate the surface area and the volume.

$s = 13$ cm. $O = \pi \cdot 25 + \pi \cdot 65 = 90\pi \approx 282.74\,\text{cm}^2$. $V = \tfrac13 \cdot \pi \cdot 25 \cdot 12 = 100\pi \approx 314.16\,\text{cm}^3$.

A party hat has a radius of 8 cm and is 15 cm high. How much card do you need (without a glue flap)?

Only the curved surface: $s = \sqrt{64 + 225} = 17$ cm, $M = \pi \cdot 8 \cdot 17 \approx 427\,\text{cm}^2$.

How much ice cream fits into the cone from example 1 ($r = 3$ cm, $h = 10$ cm) if it is filled to the brim? How much wafer do you need?

$V = \tfrac13 \cdot \pi \cdot 9 \cdot 10 = 30\pi \approx 94.2\,\text{cm}^3$. Wafer: $M = \pi \cdot 3 \cdot 10.44 \approx 98.4\,\text{cm}^2$.

A cylinder and a cone both have $r = 4$ cm and $h = 9$ cm. Calculate both volumes. How many times does the cone fit into the cylinder?

Cylinder $144\pi \approx 452.4\,\text{cm}^3$, cone $48\pi \approx 150.8\,\text{cm}^3$. Exactly three times.

A cone with a radius of 4 cm is to hold exactly 100 cm³. How high must it be?

$h = \tfrac{3V}{\pi r^2} = \tfrac{300}{16\pi} \approx 5.97$ cm

TEST YOURSELF!

Cone with $r = 3$ cm and $h = 10$ cm. Volume? Round to two decimal places.

$30\pi \approx 94.25\,\text{cm}^3$

Cone with $r = 3$ cm and $s = 5$ cm. Curved surface? Round to two decimal places.

$15\pi \approx 47.12\,\text{cm}^2$

How many times does a cone fit into the cylinder with the same radius and the same height?

Three times.

UNIT 34 LESSONS

3The sphere

All points on the surface of a sphere are the same distance from the centre, the radius $r$. A sphere cannot be unrolled like a cylinder or a cone. All the same there are simple formulas for its surface area and its volume. Archimedes found them more than 2200 years ago.

KEY POINT · THE SPHERE

Surface area: $\;O = 4\pi r^2$, four times as large as a circle with the same radius.

Volume: $\;V = \tfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3$

Radius from the volume: $\;r = \sqrt[3]{\dfrac{3V}{4\pi}}$. The cube root $\sqrt[3]{a}$ is the number that gives $a$ when cubed: $\sqrt[3]{8} = 2$, $\sqrt[3]{27} = 3$.

Calculator: the cube root has its own key $\sqrt[3]{\;}$, or you calculate $a^{(1/3)}$.

Sphere in a cylinder: the sphere fills exactly $\tfrac23$ of the cylinder that fits exactly around it.

INTERACTIVE · CALCULATING THE SPHERE

Set the radius or choose “Volume given” at the top: then the radius is calculated back with the cube root.

EXAMPLE 5 · THE FOOTBALL

A football has a radius of about 11 cm. What are its surface area and its volume?

$O = 4\pi \cdot 121 \approx 1521\,\text{cm}^2$. $\;V = \tfrac43 \pi \cdot 1331 \approx 5575\,\text{cm}^3$.

About 1521 cm² of leather and 5.6 litres of air.

EXAMPLE 6 · ONE LITRE AS A SPHERE

A sphere is to hold exactly 1 litre. What is its radius?

$V = 1000\,\text{cm}^3$: $\;r = \sqrt[3]{\tfrac{3 \cdot 1000}{4\pi}} = \sqrt[3]{238.7}$.

$r \approx 6.20$ cm

EXERCISES

A sphere has $r = 5$ cm. Calculate the surface area and the volume.

$O = 100\pi \approx 314.16\,\text{cm}^2$, $V = \tfrac{500}{3}\pi \approx 523.60\,\text{cm}^3$

A table tennis ball has a diameter of 40 mm. What are its surface area and its volume?

$r = 2$ cm: $O = 16\pi \approx 50.27\,\text{cm}^2$, $V = \tfrac{32}{3}\pi \approx 33.51\,\text{cm}^3$

The Earth is almost a sphere with $r \approx 6371$ km. What is its surface area?

$O = 4\pi \cdot 6371^2 \approx 510\,000\,000\,\text{km}^2$, that is about 510 million km².

A steel ball ($\varrho = 7.85\,\tfrac{\text{g}}{\text{cm}^3}$) has a radius of 1 cm. How heavy is it?

$V = \tfrac43 \pi \approx 4.19\,\text{cm}^3$, $m = 7.85 \cdot 4.19 \approx 32.9$ g

A sphere has the volume 268 cm³. Calculate its radius. What happens to the volume if you double the radius?

$r = \sqrt[3]{\tfrac{3 \cdot 268}{4\pi}} = \sqrt[3]{64.0} \approx 4$ cm. Double the radius: $2^3 = 8$, the volume becomes eight times as large.

TEST YOURSELF!

What is $\sqrt[3]{64}$?

$4$, because $4^3 = 64$

Volume of a sphere with $r = 3$ cm? Round to two decimal places.

$36\pi \approx 113.10\,\text{cm}^3$

Surface area of a sphere with $r = 1$ cm? Round to two decimal places.

$4\pi \approx 12.57\,\text{cm}^2$

REVIEW · DEEPEN · CONNECT

A cylinder has a volume of 90 cm³. What is the volume of a cone with the same radius and the same height?

One third: 30 cm³

Connecting with chapter 1.2: the slant height of a cone is 10 cm long and slopes at $60^\circ$ against the base. Calculate $r$, $h$ and $V$.

$r = 10 \cdot \cos 60^\circ = 5$ cm, $h = 10 \cdot \sin 60^\circ \approx 8.66$ cm, $V = \tfrac13 \cdot \pi \cdot 25 \cdot 8.66 \approx 226.7\,\text{cm}^3$.

A sphere with a diameter of 10 cm lies in a cube with an edge length of 10 cm. What percentage of the cube does it fill?

Sphere: $\tfrac43 \pi \cdot 125 \approx 523.6\,\text{cm}^3$, cube: 1000 cm³. About 52.4%.

How does the surface area of a sphere change if you triple its radius? And its volume?

Surface area: $3^2 = 9$ times as large. Volume: $3^3 = 27$ times as large.

EXCURSIONHISTORY

The tomb of Archimedes

Archimedes lived from about 287 to 212 BC in Syracuse on Sicily. He proved that a sphere fills exactly two thirds of the cylinder that fits exactly around it. And its surface area is also two thirds of the surface area of this cylinder. He was so proud of this discovery that he wished for sphere and cylinder on his tombstone.

About 140 years after his death the Roman Cicero, then an official on Sicily, searched for the tomb. He found it overgrown with thorns and brambles. He recognised it by a small column on which a sphere and a cylinder could be seen. That is how he describes it himself.

Work it out: a sphere has $r = 3$ cm. The cylinder around it has $r = 3$ cm and $h = 6$ cm. Is the ratio of the volumes right?

Sphere: $36\pi$, cylinder: $\pi \cdot 9 \cdot 6 = 54\pi$. $\;\tfrac{36}{54} = \tfrac23$ ✓

Sources: Archimedes, On the Sphere and Cylinder. Cicero, Tusculan Disputations (Tusculanae disputationes) V, 64–66.

NET

curved surface as a sector, $\varphi = 360^\circ \cdot \tfrac{r}{s}$

$r = 3$, $s = 5$: $216^\circ$

CALCULATING THE CONE

$M = \pi r s$ · $O = \pi r (r + s)$ · $V = \tfrac13 \pi r^2 h$

$r = 3$, $h = 4$: $V = 12\pi$

SPHERE

$O = 4\pi r^2$ · $V = \tfrac43 \pi r^3$ · $r = \sqrt[3]{\tfrac{3V}{4\pi}}$

1 litre: $r \approx 6.2$ cm
